slides.0.title: Sake: ingredients and brewing
slides.0.subtitle: Sake is brewed more like beer yet has wine-like finesse
slides.1.title: Ingredients
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Rice and polishing
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Sake rice varieties (such as Yamada Nishiki, Omachi, Gohyakumangoku) have a large starchy core and less protein and fat; the polishing ratio is the share left after milling, and the lower the figure, the more is milled away, usually giving a cleaner, more fragrant style
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Koji
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Koji mould (Aspergillus oryzae) is grown on steamed rice and produces enzymes that turn starch into sugar; rice has no sugar of its own, so koji is the key to sake
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Water and yeast
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Water affects fermentation and style (harder water ferments more readily for a drier style), and yeast decides the aroma type; ginjo fragrance often comes from specific yeasts
slides.1.content: Sake style starts from two numbers: polishing ratio and alcohol.
slides.2.title: The brewing process
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Multiple parallel fermentation
slides.2.highlights.0.content: As koji turns starch into sugar, yeast turns sugar into alcohol, both at once in the same tank; this yields about 15–16% alcohol, and undiluted genshu can reach about 17–20%
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The yeast starter (shubo)
slides.2.highlights.1.content: A concentrated yeast starter is made first: the modern sokujo method adds lactic acid, while traditional kimoto and yamahai rely on natural lactic bacteria for richer, tangier, gamier flavours
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Pressing, pasteurising and ageing
slides.2.highlights.2.content: After fermentation the lees are pressed off; most sake is pasteurised (hiire) twice for stability. Namazake is unpasteurised, must be kept chilled and tastes livelier
slides.2.content: Multiple parallel fermentation is sake’s biggest process difference from wine and beer and a CMS oral favourite.
